title: I've been developing a Nasdaq trading strategy using AI and TradingView. What do you think of these results?
author: Regular-External-194
selftext:
I've been experimenting with AI and TradingView Pine Script to develop a profitable trading strategy focused exclusively on the **Nasdaq New York session**.

I'm not interested in scalping. My goal is to develop a relatively simple strategy that identifies high-probability setups without requiring dozens of trades every day.

After backtesting it on NQ futures, here are the results so far for **January–September 2026**:

* **Win rate:** 45.9%
* **Profit factor:** Approximately 1.31
* **Total trades:** 122
* **Average trades per month:** 13–14
* **Profitable months:** 7 out of 9
* **Losing months:** 2 (April and August)
* **Total simulated P&L:** \+$39,120 using one NQ contract per trade

These are TradingView backtest results, not live trading performance. Commissions and slippage haven't been included yet, so actual results would be lower.

The strategy looks for setups during the New York session only. Some days have no qualifying trades, and the strategy allows a maximum of two trades per day.

I'm still testing and refining it, particularly how it performs during different market conditions.

I'm curious what more experienced traders think:

1. Is a 45% win rate with a profit factor around 1.3 good enough to build a long-term strategy around?
2. How important is having 7 profitable months out of 9?
3. Would you focus on increasing the win rate, improving the profit factor, or reducing drawdown?
4. Does anyone trade a non-scalping Nasdaq strategy during the New York session that has performed consistently better?



Would appreciate any constructive feedback or suggestions for improving the strategy.

comments.author: Fantastic-Try4083
comments.body: Not enough trades, you need a minimum of 300, ideally 1000

comments.author: wallneradam
comments.body:
PF 1.3 on 122 trades can be real. Before tuning, I'd check a few things:

1. Costs. Add commission and a tick or two of slippage in the Properties tab. 
2. Realism. Make sure every signal only uses data you'd really have at that moment. process\_orders\_on\_close fills at the signal bar's close, which you can't get live, and [request.security](http://request.security) can peek into the future if it's set up wrong. 
3. Bar Magnifier. Turn it on, so fills inside a candle are calculated from lower timeframe data. 
4. More data. Use Deep Backtesting and test it over several years, not just 9 months. 

A 45% win rate can be very good with solid risk management. Personally I'd focus on cutting the drawdown first. If the win rate goes up too, even better.

I've built strategies with a 100% win rate that survived years of backtests, then got stuck live right when it mattered. A steady win rate under 50% with a good risk/reward can make a much more stable income. So I'd watch the drawdown more than the win rate.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: 45.9% win rate with a 1.31 profit factor is workable, but those are TradingView numbers with no commissions or slippage. Add those and watch the edge shrink fast.

comments.author: ciaranwalsh96
comments.body:
The 45.9% win rate is not a problem by itself. With a profit factor of 1.31, the more important question is whether that advantage survives costs and unseen data. Roughly, that PF implies the average win is about 1.6 times the average loss, but 122 trades is still a fairly small sample and a few large winners may be doing most of the work.



Before changing the strategy to raise the win rate, I would freeze the current rules and run four checks:



1. Add realistic NQ commissions and a distribution of slippage, then double the assumed slippage as a stress test.

2. Keep the last several months completely untouched, or use a walk-forward test where every parameter choice is made only from earlier data.

3. Report maximum drawdown, time under water, average win/loss, tail loss and profit factor by month and volatility regime. “7 profitable months” is useful, but it does not show whether one month supplied most of the total profit.

4. Compare it with a simple baseline using the same session and risk budget. The question is not whether the model is profitable in isolation, but whether its complexity adds value.



I would optimize for robustness and drawdown before win rate. Increasing win rate can easily produce smaller gains and occasional larger losses. If PF stays above 1 after costs across multiple walk-forward windows and no single trade or month dominates the result, that is a much stronger reason to proceed to paper trading than the headline win rate.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: 122 trades in 9 months is a thin sample, and NQ slippage on a New York open entry is real money per contract. put one tick each way plus commissions in the strategy properties and rerun it before trusting the 7 green months.
